name: Recipes
description: Recipes: one defined combination of format, channel and surface per option, for the customer states it serves. Each recipe is held once under recipes; stages lists the recipes on each stage sheet. Journey stage and Ownership are derived (see derived_columns) and never stored. sheets holds Possibilities, a view built by make derive.

derived_columns.Journey stage: Customer States Journey stage of each of the recipe's states, in state order, without repeats
derived_columns.Ownership: Channels Ownership of each option's channel

AW-01.name: Problem-led short video
AW-01.desired_response: Watches to the end and recognises the situation shown.

metrics.note: Brand lift only with a control group.

AW-01.when: The problem or its effect can be shown in seconds, the audience uses these platforms, and you can publish steadily without paid budget.
AW-01.why_it_works: The platforms recommend videos to people who do not follow the account, so a first view needs no prior interest.
AW-01.risk: Reach depends on platform recommendation and changes without notice. Viewers have little intent, so one video rarely shows a measurable conversion. Each platform needs its own cut.
AW-01.how_to_apply: Unaware: show the situation without naming the product. Problem-aware: name the problem and one first step. Open on the situation, one idea per video, re-cut per platform.

AW-02.name: Paid reach to a defined segment

format.key: Paid Creative — cross-format: Video ad / pre-roll

AW-02.desired_response: Notices the brand and the problem it addresses.
AW-02.cta: None required. A "Learn more" link to a problem page is optional.

metrics.note: Brand lift needs a holdout group.

AW-02.when: A budget exists, the segment can be targeted on the platform (video, display, or a job-title audience on LinkedIn) and there are creatives to test. Use when organic reach is too slow.
AW-02.why_it_works: Budget and targeting decide who sees the message and when, independent of organic reach.
AW-02.risk: Exposure stops when spend stops. Repeated exposure causes fatigue. Awareness effect is not visible in clicks alone.
AW-02.how_to_apply: Define the exposed segment before launch, cap frequency, run two or three creatives and keep the strongest performer.

AW-03.name: Search-led article that answers the problem

channel.key: Earned: Search engine organic results (SEO is earned-ish)

AW-03.desired_response: Finds an answer to the question they searched and reads it.

metrics.note: Leads only when the page carries a capture offer.

AW-03.when: People already search for the problem in words you can name, and you can publish and update articles for months. Use mainly at Problem-aware; at Unaware search volume is thin.
AW-03.why_it_works: The article meets a question already being asked, so no interruption is needed, and a page keeps being found while it is kept current.
AW-03.risk: Ranking takes months and depends on competition and search engine changes. AI answers can reduce visits.
AW-03.how_to_apply: Option A is where the page is found (the search result), option B is where it is read. One question per article, answer in the first screen, link to the next-stage content.

AW-04.name: Expert byline in publications the audience reads

format.key: Written / Text: Social post / caption / thread

AW-04.desired_response: Reads the argument and links the named expert with the problem area.
AW-04.cta: None. The author bio carries a link.

metrics.note: Option C is self-published commentary: it does not carry a publication's credibility.

AW-04.when: A named person has an argument or data worth publishing and credibility matters before a buyer will talk to you. Editors accept contributed pieces in your field.
AW-04.why_it_works: Readers lend the publication's credibility to the contributor. Self-published posts build recognition with people who follow the author.
AW-04.risk: Editors decide and edit; placement is slow and hard to scale. Self-published posts reach only the author's network.
AW-04.how_to_apply: Pitch one argument with evidence, not the product. Treat options A and C as separate pieces, not one text posted twice.

AW-05.name: Guest appearance on audience-matched podcasts
AW-05.desired_response: Listens to the guest explain the problem and remembers the name or the URL.
AW-05.cta: None, or one URL or offer mentioned in the conversation.

metrics.note: Reach is host-reported. Traffic is attributed only through a dedicated URL.

AW-05.when: The audience is niche and listens to specific shows, and a speaker can explain the problem without pitching. Common for founder-led and B2B products.
AW-05.why_it_works: The host introduces the guest to listeners who trust the host and listen for long stretches.
AW-05.risk: Preparation and recording time per episode, limited scale, and weak attribution without a dedicated link.
AW-05.how_to_apply: Choose shows by audience match, offer a topic rather than the product, give one dedicated URL.

AW-06.name: Helpful participation in problem-focused communities
AW-06.desired_response: Gets a useful answer and recognises the contributor.
AW-06.cta: None. The profile carries a link.

metrics.note: A community post is not tied to leads or sales unless a tagged link is used.

AW-06.when: The audience is a niche, technical or passionate community that has its own norms and discusses the problem, and a person can contribute without selling. Option C needs a community you run.
AW-06.why_it_works: Members judge answers by usefulness, so help given in public builds recognition among people already discussing the problem.
AW-06.risk: Self-promotion breaks community rules and can lead to bans. The effort is continuous. Threads are not owned and can be removed.
AW-06.how_to_apply: Read the rules first, answer the question asked, mention the product only when it is the answer and disclose the relationship.

AW-07.name: Review profile that category researchers find
AW-07.desired_response: Sees that others use and rate the product and remembers the name.

metrics.note: Conversion rate only on visits tagged as coming from the profile.

AW-07.when: Customers exist who can be asked for reviews (see C-AD-2), and the category has review sites that people consult. At Unaware and Problem-aware the profile supports people who start exploring the category.
AW-07.why_it_works: Ratings are third-party statements shown in category listings and in search results where options are compared.
AW-07.risk: You cannot edit what reviewers write. A few reviews look weak. Sites have rules for asking and incentives. Negative reviews are public.
AW-07.how_to_apply: Complete and keep the profile current. Reviews are gathered through the review-request play, not at this stage.

AW-08.name: Live session on the problem
AW-08.desired_response: Registers, attends and asks a question.

metrics.note: Leads from attendees only when attendance is captured with contact data.

AW-08.when: The topic is one the audience will give time to, a speaker and a moderator are available, and there is a list or a partner to promote it. Option C uses a partner's audience.
AW-08.why_it_works: A live session lets people ask questions and spend time with the speaker, which a post does not.
AW-08.risk: Needs promotion. Attendance is below registrations. Preparation time is high. The replay needs a separate content unit.
AW-08.how_to_apply: Registration (Registration page) comes before the session. Publish the recording as separate content.

AW-09.name: Meme or cultural reference tied to the problem
AW-09.desired_response: Recognises the reference and shares or tags someone.

metrics.note: No downstream measure is claimed: a meme builds familiarity, not leads.

AW-09.when: The brand voice allows humour, someone can follow the cultural moment within a day, and the audience shares this kind of content. Option C suits a professional audience that jokes about its own work.
AW-09.why_it_works: A familiar reference is understood in a second and shared without explanation.
AW-09.risk: A misread tone or timing can damage the brand. References age quickly. The content teaches nothing about the problem unless the joke is about it.
AW-09.how_to_apply: Make the joke about the problem, not only the trend. Have a quick review path for tone.

AW-10.name: Press release or news story for a newsworthy event
AW-10.desired_response: Reads the news; a journalist decides to cover it.

metrics.note: Option B is the release on your own site; it is not coverage.

AW-10.when: There is a fact worth reporting (launch, original data, milestone, funding) and a list of journalists who cover the field.
AW-10.why_it_works: Coverage puts the news in front of an outlet's readers under the outlet's name.
AW-10.risk: Editors decide. Routine announcements are usually ignored. Wording and timing are outside your control.
AW-10.how_to_apply: Lead with the news and the evidence. Send to journalists who covered the topic before.

AW-11.name: Reference pages written to be cited by AI assistants

format.key: Written / Text: Pillar page / topic hub
Written / Text: Pillar page / topic hub

AW-11.desired_response: Gets a direct answer from an assistant that names your page as a source.

metrics.note: Citation counts come from sampled prompts and vary by assistant.

AW-11.when: The audience asks assistants about the problem and your pages can give a clear definition, steps and numbers. Use mainly at Problem-aware.
AW-11.why_it_works: Assistants quote clear, specific pages; a definition with sources is easier to cite than a general article.
AW-11.risk: You cannot control citations. Measurement is by sampling prompts. Assistants change how they pick sources.
AW-11.how_to_apply: Option A is the page, option B is where the answer appears (earned: the assistant produces it). Write definitions, steps and figures in plain sentences with sources.

AW-12.name: Sponsored slot in a niche newsletter or podcast
AW-12.desired_response: Reads or hears the sponsor message inside a medium they already trust.
AW-12.cta: One link or URL to a problem page or a free resource.

metrics.note: Leads counted from the sponsor link or URL only.

AW-12.when: The audience is concentrated in a few newsletters or shows, a budget exists for a test and the sponsor message can be written as useful content.
AW-12.why_it_works: The message sits in a format the audience opens on a schedule, next to content they chose.
AW-12.risk: Fixed price per issue or episode with uncertain return. Listeners and readers may skip sponsor blocks. Audience size is the publisher's claim.
AW-12.how_to_apply: Ask for audience figures, buy one issue or episode first, write the slot as an answer to the audience's question.

AW-14.name: Data or process shown as one graphic that leads to the full report
AW-14.desired_response: Understands a key figure, comparison or process at a glance, and may open the full report.

metrics.note: Downloads only if the report behind the graphic is gated. Earned mentions counts third parties that publish or embed the graphic with credit (option D).

AW-14.when: There is a data set, comparison or multi-step process that is hard to follow in text, and a fuller report or article exists to link to. At Unaware the graphic shows the figure; at Problem-aware it explains the cause or the steps.
AW-14.why_it_works: A well-built graphic carries the point in seconds and gives other publishers something to embed and cite.
AW-14.risk: A graphic with no point of its own is skipped. Figures must match the source. Text inside images is not read by search engines or screen readers unless described.
AW-14.how_to_apply: One message per graphic, the source named on it, and a text description beside it. Option D is where others embed it.

B-AW.name: Original research and expert point of view

format.key: Written / Text: Social post / caption / thread

B-AW.desired_response: Reads the finding, associates it with the company and shares it.
B-AW.cta: Read, or download if the report is gated.

metrics.note: Leads only from gated downloads.

B-AW.when: The company holds data or experience others lack, a subject expert is available, and credibility has to come before a sales conversation.
B-AW.why_it_works: Original data gives others something to cite, and a named expert gives the audience a person to follow.
B-AW.risk: Research takes weeks and budget. Findings must hold up to scrutiny. Reach needs promotion. Gating reduces readers.
B-AW.how_to_apply: Publish one finding with its method, then derive the post, deck and talk from it.

B-AW-2.name: Account-targeted ads to a named account list
B-AW-2.desired_response: Recognises the company as a source on the problem before any sales contact.
B-AW-2.cta: None. Link to a research page or a guide is optional.

metrics.note: Measure reach inside the account list, not total reach.

B-AW-2.when: Buyers are a known list of accounts, the sales cycle is long and sales wants the accounts to know the company before outreach. Different from AW-02, which targets a segment.
B-AW-2.why_it_works: Spend is limited to the people at accounts you intend to sell to.
B-AW-2.risk: A small audience limits scale and raises cost per view. Match rates for account lists vary. No direct link to deals.
B-AW-2.how_to_apply: Load the account list, target job titles per account, pair the ad with the research asset.

C-UN-1.name: Product-in-use hook video
C-UN-1.desired_response: Stops scrolling, watches and remembers the product.

metrics.note: Branded search lift needs a baseline and is not credited to one video.

C-UN-1.when: A physical or visual consumer product can show a result, transformation or use in the first seconds. Differs from AW-01, which starts from the problem.
C-UN-1.why_it_works: A strong visual hook gives the platform a reason to keep showing the video and gives the viewer a reason to finish it.
C-UN-1.risk: Hooks wear out and trends change quickly. The viewer is not looking for the product, so conversion is low per view.
C-UN-1.how_to_apply: Show the result first, explain after. Test several hooks on the same footage.

C-UN-2.name: Join a platform trend with a relevant twist
C-UN-2.desired_response: Recognises the trend, watches and shares or reuses it.

metrics.note: No downstream measure is claimed.

C-UN-2.when: A trend or sound fits the brand voice, the team can publish within a day or two, and the trend is still rising. For static jokes use AW-09.
C-UN-2.why_it_works: A trend format is already understood, so the viewer needs no explanation of the content.
C-UN-2.risk: A late or forced entry looks off-brand. Trend rights (for example music licences) vary by account type.
C-UN-2.how_to_apply: Check licence terms for sounds on business accounts before publishing.

C-UN-3.name: Creator-made sponsored video
C-UN-3.desired_response: Watches the creator use or discuss the product.
C-UN-3.cta: None. A creator link or code is optional.

metrics.note: Conversion rate only through a creator-specific link or code.

C-UN-3.when: The creator's audience matches the target, the budget covers fees and product, and the disclosure rules for the market are known.
C-UN-3.why_it_works: The audience already follows the creator and sees the product shown in the creator's own style.
C-UN-3.risk: Fees are paid before results are known. The creator controls the final content. Audiences can reject obvious ads. Disclosure is required.
C-UN-3.how_to_apply: Brief the creator on the message, not the script. Agree on disclosure wording and on what you may reuse.

C-UN-4.name: Paid short video in social feeds

format.key: Paid Creative — cross-format: Video ad / pre-roll

C-UN-4.desired_response: Watches the ad and recognises the product.

metrics.note: Brand lift needs a holdout group.

C-UN-4.when: A budget exists, the audience is defined by platform targeting, and video creative exists. Differs from AW-02, which also covers display and professional targeting.
C-UN-4.why_it_works: Paid placement in the feed gives control over who sees the video and how often.
C-UN-4.risk: Exposure stops with spend. Ad fatigue raises cost. Awareness effect is not visible in clicks.
C-UN-4.how_to_apply: Make a native-looking cut for each platform and test creatives before scaling spend.

C-UN-5.name: Feature in a consumer publication or newsletter list
C-UN-5.desired_response: Reads a recommendation from a source they trust and notices the product.

metrics.note: Traffic is attributed from referral links in the feature.

C-UN-5.when: The product fits a list or round-up format ("best for…", gift guides) and the publication or newsletter reaches the target consumer.
C-UN-5.why_it_works: A recommendation inside an editorial list carries the outlet's judgement.
C-UN-5.risk: Editors decide inclusion. Features are brief. Timing follows the publication's calendar.
C-UN-5.how_to_apply: Send a short pitch with a sample or an image set to editors of relevant lists.

C-UN-6.name: Sampling or pop-up where the audience already is
C-UN-6.desired_response: Tries the product or sees it in person and talks about it.
C-UN-6.cta: None. A sign-up or a tagged social post is optional.

metrics.note: Conversion rate needs a redeemable code or a sign-up at the event.

C-UN-6.when: The product is physical, a trial takes a minute, and the audience gathers somewhere you can reach (event, store, campus). Budget and staff for a site exist.
C-UN-6.why_it_works: Trying a product removes doubt that content cannot.
C-UN-6.risk: Cost per person reached is high. Reach is local. Results are hard to attribute without a code.
C-UN-6.how_to_apply: Give each visitor a code or sign-up path so later purchases can be traced.

AW-13.name: Paid search on problem queries
AW-13.desired_response: Clicks the ad that matches the query and reads a page that answers it.

metrics.note: CAC needs all costs and the customers attributed to the campaign.

AW-13.when: People search for the problem now, the budget allows tests, and a page answers the query. Use when SEO (AW-03) is too slow or the query is too competitive.
AW-13.why_it_works: The ad appears at the moment the person asks the question.
AW-13.risk: Cost per click rises with competition. Exposure stops when spend stops. Broad match brings unqualified traffic.
AW-13.how_to_apply: Option A is the ad, option B is the page the click lands on. Match the page to the query.

AN-PA-1.name: Free tool that gives an instant answer to a small version of the problem
AN-PA-1.desired_response: Uses the tool, gets a result for their own numbers and may save it.
AN-PA-1.cta: Use the tool. Saving the result may ask for an email address.

metrics.note: Leads only when saving the result asks for an email address.

AN-PA-1.when: People look for a quick answer or number tied to the problem (a cost, a size, a score) and it can be worked out from a few inputs.
AN-PA-1.why_it_works: A concrete result for the person's own numbers is worth returning to and linking to, so the tool is found by search and by other sites.
AN-PA-1.risk: Building and upkeep take effort. A wrong result destroys trust. Most visitors use it once and leave unless a next step is offered.
AN-PA-1.how_to_apply: Three or four inputs, one result. Show the result before asking for anything, then link it to the next-stage content.

B-AW-3.name: Technical tutorial on developer platforms
B-AW-3.desired_response: Follows the steps, solves the problem and notices the tool used.
B-AW-3.cta: None. The article ends with a link to the docs or the repository.

metrics.note: Stars and installs apply to products distributed through GitHub or a package registry.

B-AW-3.when: The buyer is a developer, the problem has a technical answer and the tool can be shown in working steps.
B-AW-3.why_it_works: Developers find and share working examples on platforms they already use.
B-AW-3.risk: A thin tutorial gets ignored or criticised. Hacker News front-page placement is not predictable.
B-AW-3.how_to_apply: Option B is a separate submission by a community member, not by the company. Publish the steps with working code.

C-PA-1.name: Search-led list or guide for a consumer problem

channel.key: Earned: Search engine organic results (SEO is earned-ish)

format.key: Written / Text: Pillar page / topic hub

C-PA-1.desired_response: Finds a list of options or steps for the problem and reads it.
C-PA-1.cta: Read. Save or subscribe is optional.

metrics.note: Engagement rate covers saves and shares.

C-PA-1.when: Consumers search the problem as "ways to…", "ideas for…" or "best…" queries, and you can keep list pages current. Differs from AW-03, which answers one question.
C-PA-1.why_it_works: List pages match a search habit and give several entry points to related content.
C-PA-1.risk: Ranking takes months and competes with large publishers. Lists need updates to stay useful.
C-PA-1.how_to_apply: Option A is where it is found; B and C are where it is read. Link every list item to deeper content.

C-PA-2.name: How-to and tips videos
C-PA-2.desired_response: Watches, learns a way to deal with the problem and saves the video.

metrics.note: Engagement rate covers saves and shares. Traffic comes from links in descriptions.

C-PA-2.when: The problem can be explained or demonstrated in a short video and people search or browse for tips. Differs from AW-01, which shows the situation but gives no steps.
C-PA-2.why_it_works: A viewer can apply a visible step immediately, which gives the video value on its own.
C-PA-2.risk: Tips are easy to copy. Platform recommendation varies. Few viewers click through.
C-PA-2.how_to_apply: Give one complete tip per video. Option A suits longer steps found through YouTube search.

C-PA-3.name: Answer questions on public Q&A sites
C-PA-3.desired_response: Gets an answer and may follow a link for more.
C-PA-3.cta: None. The profile or a relevant source link is optional.

metrics.note: Answers can rank in search; this is measured through the answer page URL, not claimed.

C-PA-3.when: Questions about the problem are asked repeatedly on these sites and someone can answer completely. Differs from AW-06, which is ongoing participation in a community.
C-PA-3.why_it_works: Answers are found by search and by people who ask the same question later.
C-PA-3.risk: Promotional answers are removed or downvoted. Question volume varies. Links may carry little traffic.
C-PA-3.how_to_apply: Answer fully in the post first; add a link only when it holds more detail.

C-PA-4.name: Guest with practical tips on consumer-interest podcasts
C-PA-4.desired_response: Listens to practical advice and remembers the guest or the brand.
C-PA-4.cta: None, or one URL mentioned once.

metrics.note: Reach is host-reported. Traffic only through a dedicated URL.

C-PA-4.when: Shows exist for the consumer interest and a spokesperson can give tips without selling. Differs from AW-05, which suits niche B2B audiences.
C-PA-4.why_it_works: Listeners hear the guest in a trusted host's voice over a long episode.
C-PA-4.risk: Time cost per episode and limited attribution.
C-PA-4.how_to_apply: Offer a tip-based topic, not the product, and give a dedicated URL.

C-PA-5.name: Tip carousels and threads

format.key: Written / Text: Social post / caption / thread

C-PA-5.desired_response: Reads the tips and saves or shares them.

metrics.note: Engagement rate covers saves and shares.

C-PA-5.when: The advice fits several short, self-contained points and the audience uses these platforms. Option B suits an audience reached on LinkedIn.
C-PA-5.why_it_works: Each swipe or post is a small step the reader can finish; saves make the content reusable.
C-PA-5.risk: Platforms favour different formats over time. Content is easy to copy. Little direct traffic.
C-PA-5.how_to_apply: One point per card or post, a clear first card, and one next step on the last.

C-SA-5.name: Quiz that recommends an option

format.key: Written / Text: Social post / caption / thread

C-SA-5.desired_response: Answers a few questions and gets a result: a diagnosis of the problem (Problem-aware) or a recommended option (Solution-aware).
C-SA-5.cta: Take the quiz. A second ask, email for the result, comes at the end.

metrics.note: Direct conversion = visit to quiz completion. Downstream = purchase from the recommendation. Define both events.

C-SA-5.when: The product range is wide enough that choice is hard and the quiz can be answered in about a minute. At Problem-aware the quiz diagnoses the problem and points to guides; at Solution-aware it recommends an option. Option B drives people to the quiz.
C-SA-5.why_it_works: The result is personal, which gives a reason to share an email address and a clear next step.
C-SA-5.risk: Recommendations must reflect real product fit. Long quizzes lose people. Consent is required for follow-up.
C-SA-5.how_to_apply: Keep to five questions or fewer and make every answer change the result.

AN-SA-1.name: Gated guide, template or toolkit
AN-SA-1.desired_response: Gives contact details to receive the asset and uses it to compare options or do the task.

metrics.note: MQL count depends on your qualification rule.

AN-SA-1.when: The buyer is comparing approaches and the asset is useful enough to be worth an email address. A follow-up sequence (AN-SA-2) is ready.
AN-SA-1.why_it_works: A useful asset gives the buyer something to keep and gives you a contact to follow up with.
AN-SA-1.risk: Gating reduces readers. A generic asset attracts unqualified contacts. Consent and privacy rules apply.
AN-SA-1.how_to_apply: Keep the form to the fields needed to follow up.

AN-SA-2.name: Email sequence after a download or sign-up
AN-SA-2.desired_response: Keeps reading and takes the next step offered.
AN-SA-2.cta: One next step per email (for example book a demo, start a trial).

metrics.note: Count a downstream result only for contacts who entered the sequence.

AN-SA-2.when: Consent to email exists, contacts come from AN-SA-1 or a sign-up, and there is content for each step.
AN-SA-2.why_it_works: A sequence delivers the next piece when the contact is still interested, without manual work.
AN-SA-2.risk: Unsubscribes if emails are generic. Consent and sending rules apply.
AN-SA-2.how_to_apply: Three to five emails, each with one purpose and one link.

AN-SA-3.name: Live session or expert interview comparing approaches
AN-SA-3.desired_response: Registers, attends and uses the session to compare approaches.

metrics.note: Leads from attendees only when attendance is captured with contact data.

AN-SA-3.when: The buyer knows solutions exist and wants to see approaches side by side, with questions answered. Differs from AW-08, which names the problem. Option C is a panel with a partner. Option D is a recorded interview with an outside expert, for buyers who will not attend live.
AN-SA-3.why_it_works: A live comparison lets the buyer ask which approach fits their case.
AN-SA-3.risk: Needs promotion and a speaker who can compare fairly. Attendance is below registrations.
AN-SA-3.how_to_apply: Show the same case worked through each approach.

AN-SA-4.name: Exhibit at an industry trade show
AN-SA-4.desired_response: Stops at the booth, talks with staff, sees a demonstration and leaves contact details or books a meeting.
AN-SA-4.cta: Scan the badge or book a meeting.

metrics.note: Count leads by badge scans at the event; credit later results only to contacts captured there.

AN-SA-4.when: Buyers in the target segment attend a specific industry event, a budget covers space and staff, and the product can be shown live in a few minutes. Use for in-person contact with many buyers in a short time; it is not a live session, which is a scheduled talk or webinar (AW-08).
AN-SA-4.why_it_works: The booth puts the product and a person in front of buyers who came to compare suppliers, and allows a conversation on the spot.
AN-SA-4.risk: Space, travel and staff cost are high. Lead quality varies. Leads go cold without fast follow-up.
AN-SA-4.how_to_apply: Option A is the booth; option B is the demonstration run there. Book follow-up meetings at the event and send the follow-up within days.

AN-SA-5.name: Recurring editorial newsletter to subscribers
AN-SA-5.desired_response: Reads each issue and replies or follows the one link.
AN-SA-5.cta: Read. Reply or click one link per issue.

metrics.note: MQL count depends on your qualification rule and counts only subscribers who meet it.

AN-SA-5.when: Subscribers want continuing insight on the options they are comparing, and someone can publish on a steady schedule on a stable topic. Differs from AN-SA-2, which is a fixed sequence after a download.
AN-SA-5.why_it_works: A regular issue keeps the company in view while the buyer compares approaches, without paid reach.
AN-SA-5.risk: Needs a steady schedule. List growth is slow. Open rate is a trend, not an exact figure. Consent and sending rules apply.
AN-SA-5.how_to_apply: One theme per issue and one main link. Reuse the strongest blog and social posts.

B-CO.name: Evidence library for evaluators
B-CO.desired_response: Finds evidence that applies to their situation and shares it with colleagues.
B-CO.cta: Download, or run the calculator or assessment. A demo request is offered after the evidence.

metrics.note: Demo requests count only when the evidence page links to them.

B-CO.when: The buyer is a team that asks "will it work for us" and "is it worth it", and real customer results can be published with permission. At Decision the ROI tool and case studies answer the budget holder's "is it worth it".
B-CO.why_it_works: Evidence tied to a situation answers the question each committee member brings.
B-CO.risk: Needs customer results the customer has approved. Unsupported claims damage trust. Gating reduces readers.
B-CO.how_to_apply: Name the customer type and result in the title. Use the ROI tool with the buyer's own numbers.

B-CO-2.name: Listings in integration directories and marketplaces

channel.key: Shared / hybrid: Marketplace / app store listings
Shared / hybrid: Claude Code plugin marketplace

B-CO-2.desired_response: Finds the product inside the ecosystem they already use and checks compatibility.

metrics.note: Installs apply where the platform reports them.

B-CO-2.when: The product integrates with platforms where buyers search for tools, and the platform accepts listings.
B-CO-2.why_it_works: Buyers search inside the platform they already work in, and the listing is found where they look.
B-CO-2.risk: The platform sets rules, review times and fees, and owns the ranking. Listings need maintenance.
B-CO-2.how_to_apply: Choose the platforms by where your buyers' tools live; one listing per platform, written for that platform's search.

C-SA-1.name: Comparison of approaches before choosing a product

channel.key: Earned: Search engine organic results (SEO is earned-ish)

C-SA-1.desired_response: Compares approaches and narrows to one.
C-SA-1.cta: Read or watch. Email capture is optional.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = visitors who reach a product page after the comparison.

C-SA-1.when: The buyer knows solutions exist and is weighing approaches (for example product types), not brands yet.
C-SA-1.why_it_works: A fair comparison of approaches helps the buyer decide and puts the product in the shortlist.
C-SA-1.risk: A biased comparison is noticed. Pages need updating as the market changes.
C-SA-1.how_to_apply: Option 1 is where the comparison is found, 2 to 4 are where it is read. Compare approaches on the criteria buyers use.

C-SA-2.name: Inclusion in third-party reviews and round-ups
C-SA-2.desired_response: Sees the product ranked or recommended among alternatives.

metrics.note: Conversion rate on visits that arrive from the review or round-up link.

C-SA-2.when: Consumers shortlist from ratings and round-ups, and the product has enough reviews or merit to be included.
C-SA-2.why_it_works: Third parties compare options on stated criteria, so inclusion is a credible shortlist signal.
C-SA-2.risk: You cannot choose rankings or wording. Paid placement in a round-up must be disclosed.
C-SA-2.how_to_apply: Supply accurate product data to editors; ask satisfied customers for reviews through C-AD-2.

C-SA-3.name: Creator review of the product against alternatives
C-SA-3.desired_response: Watches an honest review and judges whether the product suits them.
C-SA-3.cta: None. A creator link or code is optional.

metrics.note: Conversion rate only through a creator-specific link or code.

C-SA-3.when: Buyers watch reviews before choosing, and a creator who reviews this category would be credible. Option B is an unpaid review you do not control.
C-SA-3.why_it_works: Buyers use a reviewer who has tried several products as a proxy for their own trial.
C-SA-3.risk: An honest review can be negative. Paid reviews must be disclosed. Fees are paid before results are known.
C-SA-3.how_to_apply: Send the product with no script; agree on disclosure; do not edit conclusions.

C-SA-4.name: Peer recommendation threads and live Q&A
C-SA-4.desired_response: Asks which option to pick and gets answers from people who used them.

metrics.note: Leads only through a tagged link inside your own answer or session.

C-SA-4.when: Buyers ask "which one should I get" in groups, or have questions that suit a live session. Differs from AW-06: the question here is which option, not what the problem is.
C-SA-4.why_it_works: Peers answer from experience and members trust them more than the vendor.
C-SA-4.risk: Communities remove promotion. You cannot control other members' answers. Option C needs an audience that follows your page.
C-SA-4.how_to_apply: Answer the question asked, say who you are, and compare fairly.

AN-PR-1.name: Self-guided product tour or recorded demo
AN-PR-1.desired_response: Sees how the product works without talking to sales.
AN-PR-1.cta: Start a trial or book a demo at the end.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = visit to tour completion.

AN-PR-1.when: The product can be shown in a few clicks and visitors want to see it before speaking to anyone.
AN-PR-1.why_it_works: Seeing the product removes the wait for a demo.
AN-PR-1.risk: Building the tour takes effort. A tour shows a simplified path. Completion rates overstate interest.
AN-PR-1.how_to_apply: Show the main job to be done, not every feature. Option C is a recorded demo for products that cannot be toured in a few clicks.

AN-PR-2.name: Use-case and feature pages
AN-PR-2.desired_response: Finds the page for their use case and sees how the product does the job.
AN-PR-2.cta: Start a trial or book a demo.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = visit to trial or demo request.

AN-PR-2.when: The product serves several use cases that buyers search for or ask about.
AN-PR-2.why_it_works: A page per use case answers "can it do my job" without a call.
AN-PR-2.risk: Thin or repeated pages add little. Pages must change with the product.
AN-PR-2.how_to_apply: One use case per page, with a worked example and one next step.

AN-PR-3.name: Answer buying questions in a conversation
AN-PR-3.desired_response: Gets a direct answer, or is passed to a person, and books a meeting or a demo.
AN-PR-3.cta: Ask a question. Book a meeting or demo when offered.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = conversations that end in a meeting, a demo request or a sign-up.

AN-PR-3.when: Visitors on product and pricing pages have specific questions and leave unanswered, there is a knowledge base to answer from, and staff or rules exist to hand over to a person.
AN-PR-3.why_it_works: The answer arrives at the moment of the question, and serious buyers reach sales without filling in a form.
AN-PR-3.risk: A bot that cannot answer frustrates visitors. Live chat needs staffed hours. Transcripts hold personal data (consent and retention rules apply).
AN-PR-3.how_to_apply: Option A is automated, option B is staffed. Start with the ten most common pre-sales questions and offer a route to a person at every step.

B-CO-3.name: Technical documentation for evaluators
B-CO-3.desired_response: Checks whether the product meets technical requirements.
B-CO-3.cta: Start a trial or contact engineering.

metrics.note: Count only visits that start from the docs link.

B-CO-3.when: A technical evaluator takes part in the decision and checks integration, API or architecture fit before a demo (Product-aware) and again against the specification before signing (Decision).
B-CO-3.why_it_works: Evaluators trust specifics they can read without asking sales.
B-CO-3.risk: Out-of-date docs lose trust fast. Open docs may expose details you do not want public.
B-CO-3.how_to_apply: Keep one path from the product page to the docs and from the docs to a trial.

C-PR-1.name: Customer reviews where the buyer decides

format.key: Social Proof / UGC: UGC photo / video

C-PR-1.desired_response: Reads what other buyers say and judges whether the product fits.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = product-page visits to purchase. Revenue needs a stated attribution rule.

C-PR-1.when: The buyer knows the product and wants proof from people like them. Reviews exist or can be collected (C-AD-2).
C-PR-1.why_it_works: Reviews are statements from buyers with no stake in the sale.
C-PR-1.risk: A few reviews look weak. Negative reviews are public. Review rules limit incentives.
C-PR-1.how_to_apply: Show reviews near the buy decision. Option B is on sites you do not own; option C is customer content you may share with permission.

C-PR-2.name: Customer testimonial video or quote
C-PR-2.desired_response: Sees a customer like them describe a result.
C-PR-2.cta: Watch (for video). No ask for the quote.

metrics.note: Revenue needs a stated attribution rule.

C-PR-2.when: A customer has agreed to be quoted or filmed and the result is specific. Option C uses the same asset as an ad.
C-PR-2.why_it_works: A named customer with a specific result makes the claim concrete.
C-PR-2.risk: Needs customer consent and approval. Vague quotes add little. Ad use of a testimonial needs separate permission.
C-PR-2.how_to_apply: Ask for the situation before and the result after, in the customer's words.

C-PR-3.name: Unboxing and first-use videos

format.key: Social Proof / UGC: UGC photo / video

C-PR-3.desired_response: Sees the product arrive and be used, to check size, quality and contents.

metrics.note: Conversion rate only through a creator link or code.

C-PR-3.when: The buyer cannot touch the product and wants to see it in real hands. Option A is by customers; option B is paid and must be disclosed.
C-PR-3.why_it_works: Seeing the actual product reduces doubt about what arrives.
C-PR-3.risk: You do not control what a customer shows. Product and packaging flaws become visible.
C-PR-3.how_to_apply: Design packaging and the first use to be filmable; ask customers for permission to share their videos.

C-PR-4.name: Direct comparison with a named alternative
C-PR-4.desired_response: Reads how the product differs from the alternative they are considering.
C-PR-4.cta: Read. The next step (buy or start) sits on the page.
C-PR-4.when: Buyers search "X vs Y" or name a competitor in questions.
C-PR-4.why_it_works: The buyer is already comparing; a clear comparison answers the question where they ask it.
C-PR-4.risk: Claims about competitors must be accurate and current. Pages date quickly.
C-PR-4.how_to_apply: Compare on facts the buyer can check, include where the alternative is better, and date the page.

C-PR-5.name: Answers to buying objections
C-PR-5.desired_response: Gets the objection answered and continues to the buy step.

metrics.note: Revenue needs a stated attribution rule.

C-PR-5.when: Support and sales hear the same questions before purchase (delivery, sizing, returns, compatibility). At Decision the same answers sit on the pricing and checkout pages and cover price, returns and delivery.
C-PR-5.why_it_works: Answers sit where the question arises, so the buyer does not leave to ask.
C-PR-5.risk: Answers that avoid the question reduce trust. Answers must be kept current.
C-PR-5.how_to_apply: Take questions from support logs, not from guesses; answer in two sentences.

C-DE-4.name: Retargeting visitors who viewed or carted
C-DE-4.desired_response: Returns to the product they viewed and completes the purchase.

metrics.note: Test with a holdout: retargeting often credits purchases that would have happened.

C-DE-4.when: There is enough site traffic for audiences, tracking consent is in place, and the buyer left without buying. At Product-aware the ads show proof (reviews, comparisons) to people who viewed product pages; at Decision they return people who carted or started checkout.
C-DE-4.why_it_works: The ad reaches people who showed interest and shows the product they looked at.
C-DE-4.risk: Stops when spend stops. Frequent exposure annoys. Tracking consent rules apply.
C-DE-4.how_to_apply: Exclude people who already bought; cap frequency.

AN-DE-1.name: Start a trial or free plan without sales contact
AN-DE-1.desired_response: Starts a trial or free plan.

metrics.note: Activation is handled by AN-ON-1.

AN-DE-1.when: The product can be used alone within minutes and the buyer wants to try before talking to anyone.
AN-DE-1.why_it_works: Trying the product answers the buyer's doubts directly.
AN-DE-1.risk: Many trial users never activate. Support load rises. Free plans can attract users who never pay.
AN-DE-1.how_to_apply: Ask for the least information needed and send the user straight into the first step.

AN-DE-2.name: Paid search on brand and competitor terms
AN-DE-2.desired_response: Finds the product when searching its name or an alternative's name and moves to buy or trial.

metrics.note: Test with a pause on brand terms: brand clicks may have arrived without the ad.

AN-DE-2.when: Competitors bid on your name, or buyers search "X alternatives" before deciding.
AN-DE-2.why_it_works: The ad holds the result position at the moment of decision.
AN-DE-2.risk: Brand clicks often arrive anyway. Competitor terms are subject to platform and trademark policies.
AN-DE-2.how_to_apply: Option A is the ad, option B is the page it lands on.

B-DE.name: Sales-led demo, proposal and follow-up
B-DE.desired_response: Understands how the product fits their case and agrees the next step with sales.
B-DE.cta: Agree on a proposal, then sign.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = opportunity stage to the next stage.

B-DE.when: The buyer has an active opportunity with a named contact, and sales owns the conversation.
B-DE.why_it_works: Each asset answers a question the buyer raised, in the form (live, video, document) they use.
B-DE.risk: Quality varies by salesperson. Generic decks and emails are ignored. Time per opportunity is high.
B-DE.how_to_apply: Send each asset after a stated question from the buyer, and name the next step in it.

B-DE-2.name: Security and compliance review pack
B-DE-2.desired_response: The security, legal or procurement reviewer confirms the requirements are met.
B-DE-2.cta: None. Sales sends the pack on request.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = review passed to the next stage.

B-DE-2.when: The buying committee includes security, legal or procurement, and they ask for certifications, data handling and policies.
B-DE-2.why_it_works: Reviewers decide on documents they can check, not on claims.
B-DE-2.risk: Documents must be current and certifications real. A slow answer delays the deal.
B-DE-2.how_to_apply: Option A is the public trust page; option B is the full pack sent under agreement.

B-DE-3.name: Customer reference and proof of concept
B-DE-3.desired_response: Hears from a comparable customer, or sees it work on their own data.
B-DE-3.cta: Agree success criteria for the pilot.

metrics.note: Reference calls completed counts calls held, not references approved (see B-AD-1). Conversion rate = reference or pilot to the next stage.

B-DE-3.when: The committee wants peer evidence or proof on their own data before signing.
B-DE-3.why_it_works: A peer call and a working pilot answer "will it work for us" with direct evidence.
B-DE-3.risk: References tire if overused. A pilot needs scope and success criteria or it stalls.
B-DE-3.how_to_apply: Write the success criteria with the buyer before the pilot starts.

B-DE-4.name: Executive invitation: direct mail and roundtable
B-DE-4.desired_response: An executive at a target account accepts a conversation.

metrics.note: Attribution is manual; record which accounts were invited.

B-DE-4.when: Deals are large, accounts are named and the senior decision maker is hard to reach by email.
B-DE-4.why_it_works: A physical item and a small event reach people who ignore email, and give time with peers.
B-DE-4.risk: Cost per account is high, numbers are small and results are hard to attribute.
B-DE-4.how_to_apply: Invite by name and give a specific reason to attend.

C-DE-1.name: Offer with stated terms (discount or bundle)
C-DE-1.desired_response: Decides to buy at the offered price.

metrics.note: Compare against a no-offer group to see the effect of the discount.

C-DE-1.when: Price or value is the buyer's main hesitation, the margin allows an offer, and the terms can be stated clearly.
C-DE-1.why_it_works: A clear offer gives a reason to act now at a known price.
C-DE-1.risk: Discounts reduce margin and can teach customers to wait. Terms must be clear and honoured.
C-DE-1.how_to_apply: State the saving and the end condition on every content unit.

C-DE-2.name: Genuine deadline or limited stock
C-DE-2.when: Stock or the offer really ends, and buyers are ready but delaying.
C-DE-2.why_it_works: A real limit gives a reason to decide today.
C-DE-2.risk: False urgency harms trust and can break consumer law. Repeated deadlines lose force.
C-DE-2.how_to_apply: Show the actual end time or stock count, and keep the limit when it passes.

C-DE-3.name: Guarantee and return terms shown at the decision point
C-DE-3.desired_response: Feels able to buy because the risk is limited.
C-DE-3.when: Buyers hesitate about fit, quality or regret, and the terms are generous enough to state.
C-DE-3.why_it_works: A visible guarantee lowers the cost of a wrong choice.
C-DE-3.risk: Returns cost money. Terms must match the real policy.
C-DE-3.how_to_apply: Put a one-line version next to the buy button and link to the full terms.

C-DE-5.name: Total price and delivery shown before checkout
C-DE-5.desired_response: Knows the total cost and delivery date and proceeds to checkout.
C-DE-5.when: Buyers abandon when shipping, tax or delivery time appear late.
C-DE-5.why_it_works: No surprise at the last step, so the decision made on the product page holds.
C-DE-5.risk: Showing a high shipping cost early can reduce clicks to checkout.
C-DE-5.how_to_apply: Show the total and delivery date from the product page on.

B-PU-1.name: Order form and contract signature, with handover
B-PU-1.desired_response: Signs the order form (and the contract where one is not already in place) and receives a named next step.

metrics.note: Close rate = opportunities that reach signature ÷ opportunities that reach this step. Time-to-value starts at signature.

B-PU-1.when: The buyer has chosen the product. The order form records what is bought, at what price and term; the contract holds the legal terms and is needed when no master agreement exists yet.
B-PU-1.why_it_works: A clear document and a named next step keep the decision from stalling after the choice is made.
B-PU-1.risk: Legal and procurement review can delay signature. Terms in the order form must not conflict with the contract.
B-PU-1.how_to_apply: Option A is needed in every deal; option B only when there is no signed agreement. Send the kickoff date together with the documents.

C-PU-1.name: Checkout steps and payment
C-PU-1.when: A buyer has chosen the product and reaches the payment step.
C-PU-1.why_it_works: Fewer fields and clear steps remove reasons to stop.
C-PU-1.risk: Each added field or surprise loses buyers. Payment methods that buyers expect are missing.
C-PU-1.how_to_apply: Offer guest checkout and the main local payment methods; show errors next to the field.

C-PU-2.name: Order confirmation and what happens next
C-PU-2.desired_response: Knows the order is complete and what to expect.

metrics.note: Compare the contact rate with the rate before the change or with a group that got the old message. Contacts avoided are not counted; they cannot be observed.

C-PU-2.when: Every order. Buyers need confirmation and delivery information.
C-PU-2.why_it_works: Confirmation closes the decision and removes the need to ask.
C-PU-2.risk: Missing or late confirmation causes support contacts and doubt. SMS needs consent.
C-PU-2.how_to_apply: State order, delivery date and how to change it in the first lines.

C-PU-3.name: Receipt and package insert
C-PU-3.desired_response: Finds usage help, the support route or a next step.
C-PU-3.cta: None. A code or link may be printed on the insert.

metrics.note: Traffic counts only visits from the printed code or link. Contact rate is compared with orders shipped without the insert.

C-PU-3.when: A physical product ships or a receipt is sent, and there is something useful to include (setup, care, support).
C-PU-3.why_it_works: The buyer holds the insert at the moment of first use.
C-PU-3.risk: Inserts add cost and are often discarded. Tracking depends on a unique code.
C-PU-3.how_to_apply: Include one use-focused message and one way to get help.

C-PU-4.name: Add-on offer at checkout
C-PU-4.desired_response: Adds a related item to the order.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = offer accepted. Checkout completion rate is the guard: it should not fall.

C-PU-4.when: There is a related low-cost item that fits the order and does not slow payment.
C-PU-4.why_it_works: The buyer has already decided and an add-on takes one click.
C-PU-4.risk: Clutter can lower checkout completion. Irrelevant offers annoy.
C-PU-4.how_to_apply: Offer one item, shown after the payment details are entered.

C-PU-5.name: Abandoned checkout recovery
C-PU-5.desired_response: Returns to the saved cart and completes the order.

metrics.note: Count orders from recovered carts only.

C-PU-5.when: Customers leave the checkout and you hold an email address or a push consent.
C-PU-5.why_it_works: The message returns the buyer to a prepared cart.
C-PU-5.risk: Needs consent. A discount in every message teaches buyers to abandon.
C-PU-5.how_to_apply: First message within hours, no discount; add one later if needed.

AN-ON-1.name: Checklist to first value
AN-ON-1.desired_response: Completes the steps that lead to the first value.

metrics.note: Define the first-value event before measuring.

AN-ON-1.when: The product has a clear first-value event and a short list of steps that lead to it.
AN-ON-1.why_it_works: A visible list of steps shows progress and what remains.
AN-ON-1.risk: A long list discourages. The first-value event must be a real result, not a click.
AN-ON-1.how_to_apply: Three to five steps; the last is the first-value event.

B-ON-1.name: Kickoff and success plan with a named owner
B-ON-1.desired_response: Agrees the goal, the owners and the first milestones.
B-ON-1.when: The account is large enough for a customer success manager, setup needs more than one person, and a purchase goal exists.
B-ON-1.why_it_works: Agreed owners and dates make the setup a shared project.
B-ON-1.risk: Staff time per account. Plans lapse without follow-up.
B-ON-1.how_to_apply: Use the buyer's stated goal as the first milestone.

B-ON-2.name: Developer quickstart and sandbox
B-ON-2.desired_response: Makes a first successful request or integration.
B-ON-2.when: The user is a developer and first value is a working call or integration.
B-ON-2.why_it_works: A working example in a safe environment lets a developer reach first value alone.
B-ON-2.risk: The quickstart breaks when the API changes. A sandbox needs its own upkeep.
B-ON-2.how_to_apply: One copy-paste example that works, with a visible result.

C-ON-1.name: Welcome message with one first step
C-ON-1.desired_response: Opens the welcome and completes the first step.
C-ON-1.cta: Do the first step (for example set up, register the product, make a first use).
C-ON-1.when: A new customer or user has just signed up or bought and consent to message exists.
C-ON-1.why_it_works: The welcome arrives when attention to the product is highest and names a single next step.
C-ON-1.risk: A welcome with several asks gets none done. SMS needs separate consent.
C-ON-1.how_to_apply: One message, one step, sent the same day.

C-ON-2.name: In-context how-to guidance at first use
C-ON-2.desired_response: Learns how to do the task at the moment they need to do it.
C-ON-2.when: Users stall at specific points in first use, and usage data shows where. Differs from AN-ON-1, which sequences the steps to first value. At Retention the same guidance resolves problems that appear later (a feature stops working, a task changes); troubleshooting guides sit in the help center.
C-ON-2.why_it_works: Help that appears at the point of need is used more than help the user has to look for.
C-ON-2.risk: Too many prompts interrupt. Guidance goes out of date when the interface changes.
C-ON-2.how_to_apply: Add guidance only where analytics show people stall. Option E is the error message: say what happened and how to fix it, and link the help article for that error.

C-ON-3.name: Short tips series after purchase
C-ON-3.desired_response: Learns one use per message and tries the next feature.
C-ON-3.when: The product has several uses that new customers do not discover alone. Differs from C-ON-1, which is a single welcome.
C-ON-3.why_it_works: Spacing tips over the first weeks matches how people learn a product.
C-ON-3.risk: Unsubscribes if tips repeat what the customer knows. Needs consent.
C-ON-3.how_to_apply: Three to five emails over two weeks; each shows one use.

C-ON-4.name: Invitation to the customer community
C-ON-4.desired_response: Joins the community and reads or asks a first question.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = invited to joined. Retention effect needs a comparison with customers who did not join.

C-ON-4.when: An active community exists where new customers will find answers or peers. At Advocacy the invitation goes to satisfied customers to help answer other members' questions.
C-ON-4.why_it_works: Peers answer product questions and make new customers feel part of a group.
C-ON-4.risk: An empty community discourages joining. Moderation takes ongoing effort.
C-ON-4.how_to_apply: Send the invite after the first successful use, not at sign-up.

AN-RE-1.name: Prompt to try a feature the user has not used
AN-RE-1.desired_response: Tries a feature relevant to how they already use the product.

metrics.note: Retention effect needs a comparison group that did not see the prompt.

AN-RE-1.when: Usage data shows a feature linked to retention that this user has not tried.
AN-RE-1.why_it_works: The prompt is tied to the user's own use, so it is relevant.
AN-RE-1.risk: Notification fatigue. Prompts for unrelated features annoy.
AN-RE-1.how_to_apply: Show the prompt only after the user completes a related action.

AN-RE-2.name: Renewal notice and renewal conversation
AN-RE-2.desired_response: Renews with knowledge of the terms and the value received.
AN-RE-2.when: A subscription or contract ends on a known date. Option B is for accounts with a named manager.
AN-RE-2.why_it_works: A timely notice avoids lapses caused by oversight.
AN-RE-2.risk: Auto-renewal rules and notice periods are set by law and contract. A notice sent too late creates complaints.
AN-RE-2.how_to_apply: Send the first notice early enough to leave time to decide.

AN-RE-3.name: Customer feedback survey
AN-RE-3.desired_response: Answers one quick question about their experience.

metrics.note: Do not credit retention to the survey alone: compare customers who raised a problem and were helped with similar customers who were not asked.

AN-RE-3.when: Customers have used the product long enough to judge it, and someone reads and acts on the answers.
AN-RE-3.why_it_works: A short question at a natural moment collects feedback early, and low scores point to customers who need help before they leave.
AN-RE-3.risk: Survey fatigue. Scores change with timing and wording. Asking without acting damages trust.
AN-RE-3.how_to_apply: One question first, comment optional. Follow up low scores personally and use promoters for review and reference requests (C-AD-2, B-AD-1).

AN-RE-4.name: Structured learning path and certification
AN-RE-4.desired_response: Starts and completes the course and uses the product with more skill.

metrics.note: Compare completers with non-completers; completers may already be the more engaged customers.

AN-RE-4.when: The product has skills worth teaching in order, customers ask how to get more from it, and someone keeps the material current.
AN-RE-4.why_it_works: A path shows what to learn next, and a certificate gives users a reason to finish and to show their skill.
AN-RE-4.risk: Material goes out of date as the product changes. Completion is low without prompts. A certificate needs rules and upkeep.
AN-RE-4.how_to_apply: Three to five short modules, prompted from onboarding emails and in-app messages, with a certificate at the end.

AN-RE-5.name: Customer value report
AN-RE-5.desired_response: Sees the value received (usage, results) and can share it inside their organisation.

metrics.note: Retention and NRR are compared with accounts that did not receive the report.

AN-RE-5.when: The product produces numbers the customer cares about (usage, savings, output) and customers have to justify renewal. The same numbers support account reviews (B-EX) and case studies (B-AD-1).
AN-RE-5.why_it_works: Showing delivered value before renewal gives the customer something to put in front of their own decision makers.
AN-RE-5.risk: Numbers must be correct and explainable. A report that shows low use triggers churn if nobody follows up. Account data has privacy limits.
AN-RE-5.how_to_apply: Option A is the live dashboard, option B the periodic email that links to it. Send before the renewal notice (AN-RE-2).

B-RE.name: Self-serve support documentation
B-RE.desired_response: Solves the problem without contacting support and keeps using the product.

metrics.note: Self-service resolution rate is a proxy: visits followed by no support contact. Contacts avoided are not counted; they cannot be observed.

B-RE.when: Users have recurring how-to or integration questions and the support team can keep articles current.
B-RE.why_it_works: Users find the answer when they need it, at any hour.
B-RE.risk: Stale or hard-to-find articles push users to support or to leave.
B-RE.how_to_apply: Write articles from the top support questions each month.

B-RE-2.name: Customer success check-ins and office hours
B-RE-2.desired_response: Raises issues early and learns how to get more from the product.

metrics.note: Compare accounts with and without check-ins; do not credit retention to one call.

B-RE-2.when: Accounts are large enough to justify a person, or many customers share the same questions (office hours).
B-RE-2.why_it_works: A person catches problems before cancellation, and group sessions answer common questions once.
B-RE-2.risk: Staff time. Customers skip sessions without a clear agenda.
B-RE-2.how_to_apply: One-to-one for large accounts, group sessions for the rest.

C-RE-1.name: Habit-forming reminders and updates
C-RE-1.desired_response: Returns to use the product when reminded.

metrics.note: Retention effect needs a comparison group.

C-RE-1.when: There is a regular reason to return (update, streak, new content) and consent for each channel.
C-RE-1.why_it_works: A message tied to the user's own activity brings them back at the right time.
C-RE-1.risk: Notification fatigue and opt-outs. Frequency rules in Publishing Rules apply. SMS and push need consent.
C-RE-1.how_to_apply: Trigger on user activity, not on a calendar alone. Option D, the release notes, is the source for update emails: say what changed and how to try it.

C-RE-2.name: Useful content for existing customers
C-RE-2.desired_response: Finds new ways to use what they own and keeps engaging.

metrics.note: Retention effect needs a comparison with customers who did not read.

C-RE-2.when: The product has uses customers do not discover alone (recipes, tips, templates).
C-RE-2.why_it_works: Showing more uses increases the value customers get from what they already bought.
C-RE-2.risk: Content that is generic does not change behaviour. Effect on retention is hard to isolate.
C-RE-2.how_to_apply: Base topics on what the most active customers do.

C-RE-3.name: Customer community and events
C-RE-3.desired_response: Posts, answers other members and attends events.

metrics.note: Compare members with non-members; members may already be more engaged.

C-RE-3.when: Customers share a use or identity and benefit from each other's answers. At Advocacy committed customers answer other members' questions, reply in threads and run local groups; badges and recognition reward the helpers.
C-RE-3.why_it_works: Members help each other, and belonging adds a reason to stay.
C-RE-3.risk: Needs moderation and a steady flow of activity. An empty community looks worse than none.
C-RE-3.how_to_apply: Seed the community with questions and recognise active members.

C-RE-4.name: Loyalty points and rewards
C-RE-4.desired_response: Earns and redeems rewards and buys again.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = rewards redeemed per eligible member.

C-RE-4.when: Customers buy repeatedly and the margin allows a reward. At Advocacy points also reward advocacy actions (a referral, a review, a post).
C-RE-4.why_it_works: Points give a reason to return to the same seller.
C-RE-4.risk: Rewards cost margin. A complex scheme confuses. Members may buy only to earn points.
C-RE-4.how_to_apply: Show balance and next reward on each content unit.

C-RE-5.name: Replenishment reminder
C-RE-5.when: The product is consumed on a predictable cycle and the date of purchase is known.
C-RE-5.why_it_works: The reminder arrives when the customer is about to need the product again.
C-RE-5.risk: Wrong timing annoys. Needs consent. Some customers stockpile.
C-RE-5.how_to_apply: Time the reminder from average use time, and offer a one-click reorder.

AN-EX-1.name: Upgrade prompt at a usage limit or feature gate

metrics.note: Conversion rate = prompts leading to an upgrade.

AN-EX-1.when: Usage reaches a limit, or the user tries a feature on a higher plan.
AN-EX-1.why_it_works: The prompt appears at the moment the user wants more.
AN-EX-1.risk: A prompt that blocks work frustrates. Limits set too low push users to leave.
AN-EX-1.how_to_apply: Show what the user gets and the price; allow dismiss.

B-EX.name: Account review with an expansion proposal

format.key: Written / Text: Sales one-pager / battle card

B-EX.desired_response: Sees the value delivered and agrees to extend the use.

metrics.note: Conversion rate = proposals approved.

B-EX.when: The account uses the product, has results to show, and has teams or needs that the current scope does not cover.
B-EX.why_it_works: The proposal builds on measured results in the account.
B-EX.risk: Proposed without results, it reads as a sales push. Needs the right budget holder in the meeting.
B-EX.how_to_apply: Open with results measured against the original goal.

AN-RS-1.name: Win-back email sequence
AN-RS-1.desired_response: Remembers the product and returns, or says why they left.
AN-RS-1.cta: Come back, or reply with the reason.
AN-RS-1.when: Users or customers have lapsed for a defined period and you hold consent to email them.
AN-RS-1.why_it_works: A message after a lapse can reach people who forgot the product or whose need returned.
AN-RS-1.risk: Low response if the product has not changed. Emailing without consent is not allowed.
AN-RS-1.how_to_apply: Say what is new, make returning one step, and ask why they left.

B-RS-1.name: Account owner outreach to a churned account
B-RS-1.desired_response: Explains why they left and considers returning.
B-RS-1.when: A past customer account left for a known reason and has a named owner who can reach the contact.
B-RS-1.why_it_works: A personal message from the account owner can learn the reason and show what has changed.
B-RS-1.risk: Staff time. Contacts may have moved on. The reason may be a price or product gap outreach cannot fix.
B-RS-1.how_to_apply: Ask for the reason first and record it, whatever the answer.

C-RS-1.name: Win-back offer for lapsed customers

metrics.note: Compare with a no-offer group to see what the offer adds.

C-RS-1.when: Lapsed customers are price-sensitive and the margin allows an offer. Differs from AN-RS-1 by the incentive and the paid retargeting option.
C-RS-1.why_it_works: An offer gives lapsed customers a concrete reason to return now.
C-RS-1.risk: Offers cost margin and can teach customers to lapse. Retargeting needs tracking consent.
C-RS-1.how_to_apply: State the offer and the end date; exclude customers who returned.

AN-AD-1.name: Customers speak for you (webinars, podcasts, talks, guest posts)
AN-AD-1.desired_response: The customer agrees to present and tells their own story.

metrics.note: Leads from sessions only when attendance is captured.

AN-AD-1.when: Customers with a clear result are willing to speak and the audience values peers more than vendors.
AN-AD-1.why_it_works: A customer speaking about a result is heard as independent.
AN-AD-1.risk: Customers' time and approval. They say what they think. Not every event accepts customer speakers.
AN-AD-1.how_to_apply: Offer to prepare the talk with the customer and to credit them. Option D is a post the customer writes and you publish on your blog under their byline.

AN-AD-2.name: Employees share company content

format.key: Written / Text: Social post / caption / thread

AN-AD-2.desired_response: Employees share posts in their own words.

metrics.note: Traffic from employee posts needs tagged links.

AN-AD-2.when: Employees have networks that overlap the audience, are willing to share, and a social media policy exists.
AN-AD-2.why_it_works: Posts from people are read and shared more than posts from a company page.
AN-AD-2.risk: Forced sharing looks scripted. Employees post from personal accounts, so policy and disclosure rules apply.
AN-AD-2.how_to_apply: Option B is the kit sent to employees; option A is what they post. Give suggestions, not scripts.

AN-AD-3.name: Partner co-marketing and directory listings
AN-AD-3.desired_response: Partner audiences find the product through the partner's own content or directory and follow the link.
AN-AD-3.cta: Read, or follow the link to the product.

metrics.note: Count a lead for the partner that supplied it, under the lead-sharing agreement.

AN-AD-3.when: Partners and integrators have audiences that overlap the buyers and agree to feature the product. Differs from B-CO-2, which is the vendor's own listing used by evaluators.
AN-AD-3.why_it_works: A partner recommends the product to its own audience, in its own channel.
AN-AD-3.risk: Depends on the partner's priorities and calendar. Lead ownership must be agreed first. Listings need updating as products change.
AN-AD-3.how_to_apply: Option A is a joint asset published by both sides; option B is the partner's listing page for the integration.

AN-AD-4.name: Customer proof displayed on the owned site
AN-AD-4.desired_response: Customers approve the use of their logo or numbers; visitors see who else uses the product and with what result.
AN-AD-4.cta: Approve the logo or statistic (customer side).

metrics.note: Conversion rate = visits to the page that go on to a sign-up or demo request; show a change only with a before-and-after or a test.

AN-AD-4.when: Customers agree to be named and results can be stated with a source and permission.
AN-AD-4.why_it_works: Recognisable customers and specific numbers shorten the buyer's doubt on high-traffic pages. This is the display side of C-PR-2 and B-CO.
AN-AD-4.risk: Logos need written permission and must come down when a customer leaves. Unsourced numbers damage credibility. Stale proof looks careless.
AN-AD-4.how_to_apply: Get written approval for each logo and figure, keep a dated register and review it every quarter.

AN-AD-5.name: Powered-by badge on customer products and sites
AN-AD-5.desired_response: Keeps the badge in place; visitors of the customer's site can follow the link.
AN-AD-5.cta: Keep the badge. Visitors click through.

metrics.note: Count leads only from a tagged badge link.

AN-AD-5.when: Customers publish a product, widget or site where a small attribution is natural and allowed (a free plan, an embedded widget, a report).
AN-AD-5.why_it_works: Each badge is a standing link from a site the customer controls, repeated across every customer.
AN-AD-5.risk: Customers can remove it. Links may be marked nofollow. Badges on low-quality sites can harm the brand.
AN-AD-5.how_to_apply: Make the badge a condition of a free tier or an opt-in, give a one-line embed code and tag the link to track clicks.

AN-AD-6.name: Affiliate program
AN-AD-6.desired_response: Joins the program and publishes content that links to the product; visitors follow the link and buy.
AN-AD-6.cta: Join the program. Buyers use the tracked link.

metrics.note: Pay commission only on completed, non-refunded sales; credit by the affiliate link or code.

AN-AD-6.when: Publishers or creators whose audience matches the buyers want a commission, a link-tracking system exists and the margin allows a commission.
AN-AD-6.why_it_works: Affiliates are paid for completed sales, so cost follows results, and their content reaches audiences you do not.
AN-AD-6.risk: Commission cuts margin. Coupon sites can take credit for sales that would have happened anyway. Affiliates must disclose the relationship, and their claims need rules.
AN-AD-6.how_to_apply: Option A is your own program, option B runs through a network. Give each affiliate approved assets, a code and clear claims rules.

AN-AD-7.name: Insider access and recognition for committed customers
AN-AD-7.desired_response: Accepts the gift, the beta place or the advisory seat and shares, tests or advises in return.
AN-AD-7.cta: Join the beta, accept the seat, or post with the item.

metrics.note: Do not credit referrals to the gift alone; record which customers received which perk.

AN-AD-7.when: A group of customers is clearly more engaged than the rest, and the company can offer access (early features, a say in the roadmap) or recognition at reasonable cost.
AN-AD-7.why_it_works: Access and recognition make customers feel part of the product, which makes them more willing to recommend it, test it and give feedback.
AN-AD-7.risk: Perks create expectations and cost. An advisory board needs real influence or it loses members. Gifts tied to public posts must be disclosed.
AN-AD-7.how_to_apply: Option A recognises (swag), option B gives early access, option C gives influence (an advisory board). Choose by what the customers value.

B-AD-1.name: Customer reference and case-study program
B-AD-1.desired_response: Agrees to be a reference and approves the written story.
B-AD-1.cta: Agree to a case study or reference call.

metrics.note: Approved references are customers who have approved use of their name or story; reference calls actually completed are counted in B-DE-3. Close rate is credited only to deals where a reference was used.

B-AD-1.when: A customer has measurable results and a good relationship with the success manager.
B-AD-1.why_it_works: A named customer's results are used in later sales and evidence (B-CO, B-DE-3).
B-AD-1.risk: Customers may refuse or need legal approval. References tire if overused.
B-AD-1.how_to_apply: Ask at a success moment, offer a draft for approval.

C-AD-1.name: Referral program with a personal link or code
C-AD-1.desired_response: Shares the link or code with someone they know.

metrics.note: Revenue counted only for referred customers who used the link or code.

C-AD-1.when: Customers are satisfied, the product is easy to explain, and a reward for both sides fits the margin.
C-AD-1.why_it_works: A personal recommendation reaches people who trust the customer, and the reward gives a reason to send it.
C-AD-1.risk: Rewards cost margin. Abuse (self-referral) needs rules. Reward rules must be clear.
C-AD-1.how_to_apply: Options A and B are the company's own prompts to the customer; option C is the invitation the customer sends, which the customer and the company jointly run. Ask after a success moment and show the reward on the prompt.

C-AD-2.name: Review request after a good experience

metrics.note: Conversion rate on visits from review profiles, where tracked.

C-AD-2.when: A customer has had a clear success (delivery, first result, resolved ticket) and the review site allows requests.
C-AD-2.why_it_works: A short request at the right moment turns satisfaction into a public review.
C-AD-2.risk: Sites forbid reviewing only happy customers or paying for positive reviews. Requests after a bad experience bring negative reviews.
C-AD-2.how_to_apply: Option A is the request you send; option B is where the review is written.

C-AD-3.name: Prompt customers to post their own photos and videos

format.key: Social Proof / UGC: UGC photo / video
Written / Text: Social post / caption / thread

C-AD-3.desired_response: Posts their own photo or video with the product.
C-AD-3.cta: Post, with the brand tag or hashtag.

metrics.note: Customer-created posts counts posts by customers who are not paid or contracted; reposts by the brand do not count.

C-AD-3.when: The product looks good or is fun to show and customers already post. A hashtag or contest gives an extra reason.
C-AD-3.why_it_works: Customers see other customers' content as less biased than brand content.
C-AD-3.risk: You do not control what is posted. Reuse of customer content needs permission. Contest rules vary by market.
C-AD-3.how_to_apply: Option A is the prompt, B is the submission, C is the public post. Ask for permission to reuse in the submission.

C-AD-4.name: Ambassador program for committed customers
C-AD-4.desired_response: Joins the program and promotes the brand to their network.
C-AD-4.when: A group of customers already recommends the product, and you can give them rewards, access or recognition.
C-AD-4.why_it_works: Committed customers carry a recommendation with their own credibility.
C-AD-4.risk: Rewarded ambassadors must disclose the relationship. Needs management and rules for conduct.
C-AD-4.how_to_apply: Option A is the page that recruits ambassadors; option B is what they post, which is paid because they are rewarded. Start with a small invited group and clear terms.

C-AD-5.name: Share card after a milestone
C-AD-5.when: The product gives users an achievement they are proud to show (progress, result, year in review).
C-AD-5.why_it_works: People share their own results, and the card carries the brand with it.
C-AD-5.risk: Shares are low unless the milestone matters to the user. Privacy settings must be respected.
C-AD-5.how_to_apply: Pre-fill the card with the user's result and make sharing one tap.

AW-15.name: Co-hosted podcast with a peer
AW-15.desired_response: Listens to two practitioners work through a problem and remembers who explained it.
AW-15.cta: None, or one URL mentioned in the episode.

metrics.note: Plays are split across both hosts' feeds; attribution needs a dedicated URL per host.

AW-15.when: Two people with complementary expertise and audiences can hold a regular conversation on a problem both audiences have. Differs from AW-05, where the host owns the show and the guest appears once.
AW-15.why_it_works: Each host brings their own listeners, so each reaches an audience that already trusts the other host.
AW-15.risk: Both hosts must keep a recording schedule. The show belongs to both, so ending or changing it needs agreement. Attribution is weak without a dedicated link.
AW-15.how_to_apply: Agree topic range, cadence and who publishes where before the first episode. Unaware: open on a situation listeners recognise. Problem-aware: name the problem and work through one cause per episode.

AN-PA-2.name: Findings co-authored with a peer
AN-PA-2.desired_response: Reads the findings and follows one of the authors.
AN-PA-2.cta: Follow or subscribe to either author.

metrics.note: Traffic is split across both publishers' sites.

AN-PA-2.when: Two parties have each worked on the same problem and can publish what they found together, under both names. Problem-aware: the article names and explains the problem. Solution-aware: it compares the approaches each author used.
AN-PA-2.why_it_works: Two named authors from different sides of a problem carry more credibility than either alone, and each publishes to their own readers.
AN-PA-2.risk: Both parties must approve the text, which slows publishing. Findings must hold up to scrutiny from both audiences.
AN-PA-2.how_to_apply: Agree what each author contributes and what each can claim. Publish on both sites with one canonical source.

AN-SA-6.name: Joint research report
AN-SA-6.desired_response: Reads or downloads the report to compare approaches against evidence from more than one source.

metrics.note: Leads are shared only as the partners' agreement allows.

AN-SA-6.when: The buyer is comparing approaches and wants evidence, and two parties hold data or experience neither could publish alone. Differs from B-AW, which one company publishes on its own. Option B gates a whitepaper for a lead.
AN-SA-6.why_it_works: Combined data covers more cases than one company's, and a partner's name makes the findings harder to dismiss as marketing.
AN-SA-6.risk: Research takes weeks, and both parties must agree on method and findings. Lead sharing needs a written agreement. Gating reduces readers.
AN-SA-6.how_to_apply: Agree the question, the data each side contributes and who owns the leads before starting. Release on both sites on the same day.

AW-16.name: Guest issue in a partner's newsletter
AW-16.desired_response: Reads the guest issue and subscribes to the guest's own list.

metrics.note: Open and click figures come from the partner and cover only their list.

AW-16.when: A partner sends a newsletter to readers who share the problem, and you can write an issue that is useful in its own right. Differs from AW-12, a paid slot, and AN-SA-5, your own list.
AW-16.why_it_works: The partner's subscribers read the issue as part of a newsletter they chose, so the guest borrows that trust.
AW-16.risk: The partner decides whether and when it runs and may edit it. One issue rarely grows a list; it needs repeating with more partners.
AW-16.how_to_apply: Offer an issue on a topic the partner's readers ask about, with one link to a page that continues it. Problem-aware: name the problem. Solution-aware: compare approaches.

AN-SA-7.name: Joint workshop at a partner's event
AN-SA-7.desired_response: Attends and works through a method on their own case.

metrics.note: Attendee contact data is shared only as the event agreement allows.

AN-SA-7.when: A partner runs an event for people comparing approaches, and the workshop can teach a method attendees use on their own case. Option B is a joint talk on the partner's stage. Differs from AN-SA-3, which you host.
AN-SA-7.why_it_works: Attendees practise the approach with someone who knows it, and the partner's event brings people you could not gather yourself.
AN-SA-7.risk: The partner sets the date, format and audience. Preparation time is high. Contact data depends on the agreement.
AN-SA-7.how_to_apply: Design the session around one case attendees bring. Agree before the event how registrations and follow-up are shared.

AN-SA-8.name: Guide co-published with a complementary product
AN-SA-8.desired_response: Downloads the guide to see how two complementary approaches fit together.

metrics.note: Leads are shared only as the partners' agreement allows.

AN-SA-8.when: Two products or practices serve the same buyer at adjacent steps, and a guide can show how they work together. Option B is a gated co-branded whitepaper.
AN-SA-8.why_it_works: Each partner promotes the guide to its own audience, and the buyer sees one combined approach instead of two separate pitches.
AN-SA-8.risk: Both brands must approve content and design. A guide that reads as two pitches is ignored. Lead sharing needs agreement.
AN-SA-8.how_to_apply: Write around the buyer's task across both steps, not around either product. Each partner hosts the asset and promotes it to its own list.
